summary: Describes requirements and mechanisms for telling a traffic-engineered MPLS or GMPLS network that a link or router will soon be turned off. The aim is to cut or avoid traffic disruption during planned maintenance. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before closing a road for repairs, you put up signs so drivers can take another way and not get stuck.

questions: how to shut down a te link without traffic loss
what is graceful shutdown in mpls
how to shut down mpls link without traffic loss
subtitle: Notifying networks when traffic-engineered links need maintenance without disrupting traffic.

tldr.problem: When MPLS networks need to shut down a link or router for maintenance, abruptly removing it disrupts ongoing traffic. Networks need a way to gracefully move traffic elsewhere before the maintenance begins.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two-phase shutdown: first, routing protocols advertise the resource as unavailable to discourage new connections; second, RSVP-TE signaling explicitly tells routers carrying traffic on that resource to find alternative paths.
tldr.outcome: Traffic can be rerouted away from the resource being shut down, avoiding the packet loss and connection disruption that would occur with an unannounced failure.

facts.label: Resource types
facts.value: Single link, component link, label resource, or entire node

today: RFC 5817 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. It is still the standard reference for graceful shutdown procedures in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When a network operator needs to take a link or router offline for maintenance—such as hardware upgrades, software updates, or repairs—the usual approach is just to shut it down. Unplanned failures trigger automatic rerouting, but it is slow and causes packet loss and connection disruption. Planned maintenance is different: the operator knows in advance when the resource will be unavailable. This document describes how to notify the network ahead of time, so traffic can move to alternative paths before the resource goes down.

Graceful shutdown is a two-step process. First, the operator signals to the network that the resource will soon be unavailable, using existing routing protocol mechanisms. Second, after a delay to allow traffic to reroute, the resource is removed from service.
sections.eli5: An operator planning maintenance wants to move traffic away first, then shut down the link. The RFC explains how to tell the rest of the network the link is closing, so traffic finds a new path automatically.

sections.title: Why Graceful Shutdown Matters
sections.content:
The RFC applies to MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks, where traffic is explicitly routed along chosen paths rather than discovered hop-by-hop. When a link unexpectedly fails, the network reroutes around it, but there is packet loss during the failover. For planned shutdowns, graceful shutdown minimizes or eliminates that loss by moving traffic first.

Graceful shutdown handles various scenarios: shutting down a single traffic-engineered link, a bundled link (a group of physical links treated as one), a label resource (in optical networks), or an entire router. The mechanism also works for multi-domain networks, where one domain signals to another that a resource is going down.
sections.eli5: Traffic-engineered networks plan the exact path packets take. Graceful shutdown tells those routers 'stop planning new paths through this link', giving old traffic time to find a new path before you remove it.

sections.title: How Graceful Shutdown Works
sections.content:
Graceful shutdown has two main phases. In the first phase, the router initiating shutdown sends routing protocol updates (OSPF or IS-IS messages) that advertise the resource as unavailable. The updates set the Traffic Engineering metric to the maximum value (0xffffffff) and the available bandwidth to zero, making the link unattractive for new path computations. Neighboring routers see these updates and stop using the resource for new traffic-engineered Label Switched Paths (LSPs).

After a delay to allow the network to stabilize and existing traffic to reroute, the second phase begins: the router sends RSVP-TE error messages (PathErr with error code "Notify") to ingress routers currently sending traffic over the resource. These messages tell the ingress routers to compute alternative paths and establish new LSPs. Ingress routers must avoid the resource that is being shut down when computing these new paths.
sections.eli5: Step 1: Tell the network 'this link is closing'. Step 2: Wait for traffic to move. Step 3: Tell the routers using the link to find a new path. Once the traffic has moved, the link can safely go down.

sections.title: Addressing Across Domains
sections.content:
For multi-domain networks, OSPF/IS-IS flooding is limited to a single domain area. The RSVP-TE signaling approach handles this better because RSVP messages are sent directly to ingress routers along LSP paths, bypassing area restrictions. When a resource in one domain is shut down, it can still notify ingress routers in other domains to reroute their traffic.

The RFC distinguishes between different types of resources being shut down: an unbundled link, a component link within a bundled link (which allows other components to keep operating), a label resource (in optical networks), or an entire node. Each scenario follows slightly different procedures in the RSVP-TE signaling phase, but the overall two-phase approach remains the same.
sections.eli5: Some networks are divided into regions. If one region's link goes down, the mechanism tells routers in other regions about it so they reroute too, even though the regions don't normally share all network information.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new security vulnerabilities; it uses existing OSPF, IS-IS, and RSVP-TE mechanisms that are already protected by existing security frameworks. Operators should apply the same protections to graceful shutdown messages as they do to regular routing and signaling messages.

Deployment considerations include monitoring (using SNMP traps when a link goes down) and the decision about how long to wait between the routing protocol update and the RSVP-TE signaling phase. A longer delay allows more time for traffic to reroute naturally, while a shorter delay means the resource comes down sooner. This timing is left as a local policy decision at the router performing the shutdown.
sections.eli5: The security relies on protecting the messages from tampering, just like regular network updates. Operators choose how long to wait between announcing the shutdown and actually removing the resource.
